experiment.rationale: This design creates two orthogonal quantitative dissociations between Take-The-Best (TTB) and Tallying, using 5 cues with well-spread validities (0.95, 0.85, 0.75, 0.65, 0.55). DISSOCIATION 1 (graded vs. flat dose-response curve): Trials C1-C3 hold the TTB-relevant structure constant (the top cue v=0.95 favors A, so TTB always picks A with probability (1-eps)*sigmoid(beta)+eps/2) while systematically increasing the number of lower-validity cues favoring B (tally margins 1-vs-2, 1-vs-3, 1-vs-4). TTB predicts a FLAT p(A) across these three trial types — the number of opposing low-validity cues is irrelevant to a one-reason rule. Tallying predicts a strictly MONOTONE DECREASING p(A) = sigmoid(-k*beta) for k=1,2,3 — a graded dose-response in tally margin. Trials C5-C7 mirror this with B favored by the top cue (TTB flat-high p(B); Tallying increasingly favors A). This is a pure quantitative dissociation: the slope of p(choice) against tally margin is exactly 0 for TTB and strictly negative for Tallying at any beta > 0. DISSOCIATION 2 (parameter-free point prediction): Trials T1-T4 have equal tallies (1 win each) but a clear validity-ordered discriminator (e.g., T1: A wins the v=0.95 cue, B wins only the v=0.55 cue). Tallying MUST predict exactly p(A)=0.50 on these trials for ALL parameter values (the softmax over tied scores is uniform, and the lapse also injects uniform). TTB predicts p(A) = (1-eps)*sigmoid(beta)+eps/2, which is strictly above 0.50 for any beta>0. Thus, if subjects choose systematically (not at chance) on T1/T3 (toward A) or T2/T4 (toward B), Tallying is falsified outright with no free parameters to rescue it — an adversarial knife. Trials G1-G2 are agreement controls (both theories pick the same option) that anchor the noise parameters. 12 unique pairs x K=8 = 96 trials per subject. Note the design also avoids any all-tie (fully degenerate) trials.

metric.rationale: This is a per-trial dissociation score exploiting both orthogonal dissociations in the design, rewritten as flat, dependency-free code (no imports, no nested functions, no try/except, no lambdas) to eliminate the transmission-level syntax failures of the previous two attempts. Construction: on each trial I compute (i) the TTB pick — the features are listed in descending-validity order (validities [0.95, 0.85, 0.75, 0.65, 0.5]), so the TTB cascade is just the lowest-index feature on which the two options differ — and (ii) the Tallying pick from strict feature-wise win counts. Trials where both theories agree (types 11-12, 16 trials/subject) are skipped. On full dissociation trials (types 1-6, 48 trials/subject), where TTB backs the option with FEWER cue wins and Tallying backs the majority-tally option, a choice matching TTB contributes +1 and one matching Tallying contributes -1. On tied-tally trials (types 7-10, 32 trials/subject), Tallying is structurally forced to exactly p=0.5 for every parameter value (softmax over tied scores is uniform and the lapse injects uniform), so any systematic choice is pure TTB signal: +0.5 toward TTB's pick, -0.5 away. Expected value under TTB-simulated data is 0.8*(2q-1) with q=(1-eps)*sigmoid(beta)+eps/2, which is strictly positive for any beta>0, eps<0.5; under Tallying-simulated data it is -0.6*avg(2p_margin-1), strictly negative for any beta>0. The mean gap is order 0.3-1.0 across plausible parameters while per-subject sd is only ~0.05-0.10 (80 informative trials pooled), giving a decisive Welch's t-test at N=25. The score is self-hedging: if TTB is simulated with weak beta, the tied-trial component still adds signal while dissociation trials shrink, and vice versa for weak Tallying parameters. The function is a simple mean of per-trial contributions, so it works identically on the pooled DataFrame and on single-subject slices, making the between-subject variance well defined.

proposer_theory.description: People compare two options by consulting cues one at a time in order of validity, stopping at the first cue that discriminates between the two options. That cue alone determines the choice: the option with the higher value on the discriminating cue wins, and no other cue is consulted. Cues with lower validity are never reached when a higher-validity cue already discriminates, so Take The Best is a "one-reason" decision rule — only a single feature is ever used on any given choice. Because only the sign of the comparison on the top discriminating cue matters, TTB ignores both the magnitude of that difference and all information on lower-validity cues, making it maximally frugal in the use of evidence. Cue validities are subjective and can be learned, inferred from instructions, or fixed by task structure. When no cue discriminates (all feature-wise comparisons tie) the learner has no basis for preference and must guess. Response noise enters through a softmax over the binary TTB score (winner = 1, loser = 0) with inverse temperature beta, plus an independent lapse that with probability epsilon replaces the softmax output with a uniform pick over the two options.
proposer_theory.predict_source:
def predict(parameters, stimulus, history):
    # Paper-faithful Take The Best (Gigerenzer & Goldstein 1996).
    # Stimulus is the pair of option feature vectors for the current
    # trial: array-like of shape (2, n_features), row 0 = option A,
    # row 1 = option B. Cue cascade: features are consulted in order
    # of descending validity; the first discriminating cue (strict
    # inequality) determines the winner; if no cue discriminates,
    # the model guesses uniformly. History is ignored.
    stim = np.asarray(stimulus, dtype=float)
    if stim.ndim != 2 or stim.shape[0] != 2:
        raise ValueError(
            f"TTB expects a (2, n_features) stimulus; got shape {stim.shape}."
        )
    n_features = stim.shape[1]

    val = np.asarray(parameters["validities"], dtype=float)
    if val.shape[0] != n_features:
        raise ValueError(
            f"validities length {val.shape[0]} != n_features {n_features}."
        )
    # Descending validity; argsort is stable so validity ties break
    # toward the earlier feature index.
    cue_order = np.argsort(-val, kind="stable").tolist()

    a, b = stim[0], stim[1]
    winner = None
    for j in cue_order:
        if a[j] > b[j]:
            winner = 0
            break
        if b[j] > a[j]:
            winner = 1
            break

    if winner is None:
        # No discriminating cue — pure guess.
        return np.ones(2) / 2.0

    scores = np.array([1.0, 0.0]) if winner == 0 else np.array([0.0, 1.0])

    beta = float(parameters["beta"])
    epsilon = float(parameters["epsilon"])

    # Softmax with max-subtraction for numerical stability. For the
    # binary TTB score this collapses to sigmoid(beta) for the winner,
    # giving a direct mapping from beta onto the paper's flip-noise
    # levels (beta=0 ↔ 50/50; beta ≫ 1 ↔ deterministic).
    z = beta * (scores - scores.max())
    e = np.exp(z)
    p_core = e / e.sum()

    n_opts = p_core.shape[0]
    return (1.0 - epsilon) * p_core + epsilon * (np.ones(n_opts) / n_opts)

experiment.rationale: This design implements a fully crossed TWO-FACTOR double dissociation between Tallying and Take-The-Best (TTB), which is structurally stronger than a one-dimensional dose-response: each theory predicts a main effect of exactly one factor and a PARAMETER-FREE ZERO effect of the other. Factor 1 is the tally margin d = (A's cue wins) - (B's cue wins), the only thing Tallying's prediction depends on: p_Tally(A) = (1-eps)*sigmoid(beta*d) + eps/2. Factor 2 is the direction s of the highest-validity discriminating cue, the only thing TTB's prediction depends on: p_TTB(A) = (1-eps)*sigmoid(beta*s) + eps/2. The 16 pairs cross d in {-4,-3,-2,-1,0,+1,+2,+3,+4} with s in {+1,-1}. KEY QUANTITATIVE PREDICTIONS: (1) WITHIN-COLUMN FLATNESS falsifies TTB with no free parameters: trials P1-P6, P13, P15 all have s=+1 (top cue v=0.92 favors A), so TTB predicts the IDENTICAL p(A) on all eight for every (beta, eps). Yet d ranges from +4 (P15: A wins 5 of 6 cues) to -4 (P6: A wins ONLY the top cue, B wins the other five). Tallying predicts p(A) falling from ~(1-eps) to ~eps/2 across these same trials. If subjects' p(A) on P6 is any lower than on P15, TTB is falsified outright -- no parameters can rescue a flat function that is observed to slope. The s=-1 column (P7-P12, P14, P16) mirrors this. (2) WITHIN-ROW FLATNESS falsifies Tallying with no free parameters: matched pairs (P2,P11), (P3,P10), (P4,P9), (P5,P8) share the same d with s flipped, so Tallying predicts EXACTLY equal p(A) within each pair for all (beta, eps), while TTB predicts a swing of (1-eps)*(2*sigmoid(beta)-1) -- up to nearly 1.0. The d=0 knife pair (P13, P14) is even sharper: Tallying must predict exactly 0.50 on both (tied tallies give a uniform softmax for any beta, and the lapse also injects uniform), while TTB predicts symmetric deviations toward the top-cue winner. (3) GRADED DOSE-RESPONSE: within each column, Tallying predicts a strictly monotone p(A) in d (sigmoid(beta*d) for d = -4..+4), giving a 9-point psychometric curve at fixed TTB output; TTB predicts a horizontal line. Conversely, across columns at fixed d, TTB predicts the full sigmoid swing while Tallying predicts zero. (4) EVEN THE AGREEMENT TRIALS SEPARATE QUANTITATIVELY: on P15 (d=+4, s=+1) both theories choose A, but Tallying predicts sigmoid(4*beta) vs TTB's sigmoid(beta) -- e.g., at beta=1, 0.982 vs 0.731 -- so confidence on unambiguous trials discriminates the theories too. As an adversarial touch against my own advocated theory, cues are displayed in descending-validity order (0.92 first), which maximally favors TTB's serial search (display order matches its search order) while being irrelevant to Tallying; if Tallying still wins under TTB's best-case display, the evidence is stronger. 16 unique pairs x K=6 = 96 trials; A/B sides are balanced (8 trials TTB-favors-A, 8 TTB-favors-B; 7 tally-favors-each-side, 2 tied), P15/P16 and P6/P12 are label-swapped mirrors that control side bias, no all-tie trials, and every pair requires genuine cue comparison.

metric.metric_source:
def metric(data: pd.DataFrame) -> float:
    # Dual-dissociation regression metric.
    # Per trial, compute:
    #   d = tally margin  = (#features A wins) - (#features B wins)
    #   s = top-cue direction = sign(A[0] - B[0])   (feature 0 has the
    #       highest validity 0.92, and every designed pair discriminates on it)
    # Regress chose-A on [1, d, s] via OLS and return b_d - b_s.
    # Tallying: choice probability depends only on d  -> b_d > 0, b_s = 0 -> metric > 0.
    # TTB: choice probability depends only on s       -> b_d = 0, b_s > 0 -> metric < 0.
    # The two theories push this scalar in opposite directions, and the
    # partial regression cleanly removes the design's d-s correlation.
    df = data.reset_index(drop=True)

    A = np.stack([np.asarray(list(r), dtype=float) for r in df["option_a_ratings"].values])
    B = np.stack([np.asarray(list(r), dtype=float) for r in df["option_b_ratings"].values])

    # Tally margin: strict feature-wise wins; ties count for neither side.
    d = (A > B).sum(axis=1).astype(float) - (B > A).sum(axis=1).astype(float)

    # Direction of the highest-validity (top) cue, which always discriminates
    # in this design: +1 if it favors A, -1 if it favors B.
    s = np.sign(A[:, 0] - B[:, 0])

    # Chose-A indicator (response: 0 = A, 1 = B).
    y = 1.0 - df["response"].to_numpy(dtype=float)

    X = np.column_stack([np.ones(len(y)), d, s])
    coef, _, _, _ = np.linalg.lstsq(X, y, rcond=None)
    b_d = float(coef[1])
    b_s = float(coef[2])

    # Tallying's signature (slope in d) minus TTB's signature (slope in s).
    return b_d - b_s
metric.rationale: The design factorially crosses the tally margin d (the ONLY input Tallying's prediction depends on) with the top-cue direction s (the ONLY input TTB's prediction depends on). I exploit both main effects simultaneously with a single OLS coefficient contrast: regress the chose-A indicator on [intercept, d, s] over all trials and return b_d - b_s. Under Tallying, p(A) = (1-eps)*sigmoid(beta*d) + eps/2, so the partial slope on d is strictly positive (up to ~0.125 per unit d when beta is large) while the partial slope on s is exactly 0 — s adds nothing once d is controlled. Under TTB, p(A) = (1-eps)*sigmoid(beta*s) + eps/2, so the partial slope on s is strictly positive (up to 0.5) while the partial slope on d is exactly 0 — within a fixed s-column TTB is flat in d by construction, and no (beta, eps) can change that. Hence the metric is positive under Tallying and negative under TTB, with a gap equal to the SUM of the two theories' signature effect sizes, making it robust: it discriminates even if one theory happens to be simulated with weak parameters, as long as the other shows its signature. Including s as a regressor also removes the mild d-s collinearity built into the 16 pairs (corr ~ 0.3), so the d-coefficient is a clean within-column slope rather than a confounded marginal. Per-subject computation is well-conditioned: every subject sees all 16 pair types x 6 reps (96 trials), d spans -4..+4 within each s-column, and the regressors are balanced (mean d = 0, eight s=+1 and eight s=-1 types). Per-subject sampling noise of b_d is small (~0.02) because it borrows strength across all nine d levels, and noise on b_s (~0.11 worst case, p=0.5) is dwarfed by TTB's s-effect (~0.5 at moderate beta). At N=25 the Welch t-test on the pooled point estimates with these between-subject variances yields a highly significant separation in every non-degenerate parameter regime.

proposer_theory.description: People compare two options by counting, across all features, how often one option has a higher value than the other. The option that wins on more features is chosen. Tallying discards cardinal magnitudes — only the sign of each feature-wise comparison matters — so the heuristic is robust to monotone rescaling of individual features and cannot be swayed by a single large feature difference in the way Equal-Weight can. Ties on an individual feature contribute nothing to either count: that cue is simply treated as uninformative for the pair. No feature is privileged, in contrast to Take The Best; every cue contributes equally to the tally. When the two counts are equal the heuristic has no basis for preference and the learner must guess. Response noise enters through a softmax over the two tallies with inverse temperature beta (interpolating between fully deterministic choice at large beta and uniform guessing at beta = 0), plus an independent lapse that with probability epsilon replaces the softmax output with a uniform pick over the two options.
proposer_theory.predict_source:
def predict(parameters, stimulus, history):
    # Paper-faithful Tallying heuristic (Dawes 1979; Gigerenzer &
    # Goldstein 1999). Stimulus is the pair of option feature vectors
    # for the current trial: array-like of shape (2, n_features),
    # with row 0 = option A, row 1 = option B. History is ignored.
    stim = np.asarray(stimulus, dtype=float)
    if stim.ndim != 2 or stim.shape[0] != 2:
        raise ValueError(
            f"Tallying expects a (2, n_features) stimulus; got shape {stim.shape}."
        )

    a, b = stim[0], stim[1]
    # Count strict feature-wise wins; ties contribute to neither option.
    a_wins = float(np.sum(a > b))
    b_wins = float(np.sum(b > a))
    scores = np.array([a_wins, b_wins])

    beta = float(parameters["beta"])
    epsilon = float(parameters["epsilon"])

    # Softmax with max-subtraction for numerical stability. When
    # a_wins == b_wins the softmax is exactly uniform regardless of
    # beta, which is the correct behavior for an undiscriminating
    # tally.
    z = beta * (scores - scores.max())
    e = np.exp(z)
    p_core = e / e.sum()

    n_opts = p_core.shape[0]
    return (1.0 - epsilon) * p_core + epsilon * (np.ones(n_opts) / n_opts)

next_theory.description: Validity-Weighted Tallying (graded-evidence regime): people integrate evidence from ALL binary expert ratings, casting each feature a sign vote (+1 win / -1 loss / 0 tie) weighted by w_j = validity_j^gamma, summing into a zero-sum evidence score, with choice a softmax (inverse temperature beta) over the two scores plus an independent uniform lapse (epsilon). The theoretical claim added this round is about where humans sit in this family: in the UNSATURATED softmax regime. Because the evidence scores are integer-scale sign tallies, beta >= 3 already drives tanh(beta*m) ~ 1 for every unit margin, making the model behaviorally deterministic and pinning it to the tallying corner; the graded dose-response in tally margin that both experiments demand (Exp 1 metric at 44% of the deterministic-tally value; Exp 2's small positive b_d) lives at beta ~ 0.2-0.3, where p(A) is approximately linear in the tally margin. Gamma stays in a mild, provably sub-lexicographic band so that no subject leaps into the TTB regime.
next_theory.predict_source:
def predict(parameters, state, history):
    # Validity-Weighted Tallying.
    # Stimulus: array of shape (2, n_features); row 0 = option A,
    # row 1 = option B; entries are binary expert ratings.
    # Each feature j casts a vote sign(a_j - b_j) for A's score and
    # the opposite for B's score; votes are weighted by w_j =
    # validity_j ** gamma. gamma = 0 -> unweighted Tallying;
    # gamma -> large -> lexicographic TTB (top cue dominates).
    stim = np.asarray(state, dtype=float)
    if stim.ndim != 2 or stim.shape[0] != 2:
        raise ValueError(
            f"Expects a (2, n_features) stimulus; got shape {stim.shape}."
        )

    n_features = stim.shape[1]
    val = np.asarray(parameters["validities"], dtype=float)
    if val.shape[0] != n_features:
        raise ValueError(
            f"validities length {val.shape[0]} != n_features {n_features}."
        )

    gamma = float(parameters["gamma"])
    beta = float(parameters["beta"])
    epsilon = float(parameters["epsilon"])

    a, b = stim[0], stim[1]

    # Feature-wise votes: +1 where A wins the feature, -1 where B
    # wins, 0 on ties (a tied cue is uninformative for the pair).
    votes = np.sign(a - b)

    # Validity-based weights. Since validities are in [0.5, 1.0],
    # gamma = 0 gives all-ones weights (pure Tallying); increasing
    # gamma increasingly privileges high-validity cues, with the
    # top cue dominating as gamma grows (TTB limit).
    w = np.power(val, gamma)

    # Weighted evidence scores. B's score is the mirror of A's
    # because every vote is zero-sum across the two options.
    s_a = float(np.dot(w, votes))
    scores = np.array([s_a, -s_a])

    # Numerically stable softmax over the two weighted scores.
    # When all cues tie (s_a == 0) the softmax is exactly uniform,
    # which is the correct behavior for an undiscriminating tally.
    z = beta * (scores - scores.max())
    e = np.exp(z)
    p_core = e / e.sum()

    # Independent lapse: with probability epsilon output a uniform
    # pick over the two options.
    n_opts = p_core.shape[0]
    return (1.0 - epsilon) * p_core + epsilon * (np.ones(n_opts) / n_opts)
next_theory.rationale: This is a minimal-diff edit of the running-best (iter 3, ACCEPTED, loss 0.1606) candidate: the mechanism code is byte-identical (w_j = validity_j^gamma sign votes, zero-sum scores, stable softmax, uniform lapse); ONLY the parameter ranges change. Why I deviate from the critic's specific numbers (beta capped 3-5, epsilon floored 0.03-0.05, gamma in [0.2, 1.0]): with zero-sum sign-vote scores the softmax input is the integer tally margin m, so p(A) = sigmoid(2*beta*m) and, in the sub-flip gamma regime, Exp 1's metric is exactly -(1-epsilon)*(1/6)[tanh(beta) + tanh(2*beta) + tanh(3*beta)]. At beta = 3 this already equals -0.4995 -- indistinguishable from beta = 10 -- so capping beta at 3-5 and flooring epsilon at 0.03-0.05 leaves Exp 1 pinned at ~-0.45 (the iter-3 corner), moving it at most ~0.02 toward the real -0.218; the gate would reject. The lever the critic's diagnosis points at but its numbers don't reach is the UNSATURATED softmax regime: the real Exp 1 value (-0.218 = 44% of the deterministic-tally value -0.50) requires (1/6)*sum(tanh(k*beta)) ~ 0.44, i.e. beta ~ 0.24; independently, Exp 2's b_d must equal ~0.077, and b_d(beta) ~ 0.08 exactly at beta ~ 0.2 (b_d(0.1)=0.048, b_d(0.23)=0.091, b_d(0.5)=0.128 on the Exp 2 design). Both experiments' targets sit in the SAME low-beta band -- a joint consistency check that this is where the data live, and precisely the 'graded dose-response in tally margin' the arbiter prescribed this family to capture (at beta ~ 0.25, p(A) ~ 0.5 + 0.24*d, linear in margin). Hence beta: [0.03, 0.55]. Variance: the critic correctly flagged that iter 3 undershot the between-subject variances (0.0050 / 0.0008 vs real 0.0140 / 0.0031). With per-subject parameter sampling, spreading beta over [0.03, 0.55] makes subject-level Exp 1 metrics range from ~-0.03 to ~-0.36 (between-subject sd ~ 0.10, var ~ 0.010) which, added to within-subject binomial noise (~0.005), lands at ~0.013-0.015 -- matching the real 0.0140 without iter 1's blowup (0.0635, caused by gamma wandering across cue-flip thresholds). Gamma stays in a mild band [0.05, 0.7]: for validities in [0.5, 1.0], at any gamma <= 1 two opposing cues always out-weigh one top cue (2*0.5^gamma >= 1 >= v0^gamma), so no simulated subject can flip into the TTB regime that ruined iter 1; gamma instead gently compresses the weighted margins at low beta and injects the small top-cue effect (b_s > 0 in Exp 2) that trims +0.124 toward +0.077. Epsilon stays small ([0.0, 0.08], mean attenuation ~4%) so it calibrates rather than drives. Expected landing zone: Exp 1 ~ -0.21 (var ~ 0.013) and Exp 2 ~ +0.08 (var ~ 0.002) vs real (-0.218, 0.0140) / (+0.077, 0.0031) -- an order-of-magnitude improvement over the base's deltas (+0.243 / +0.047), with every deviation the critic listed (Exp 1 overshoot, both variance undershoots) moved in the correcting direction.

experiment.rationale: CORE LOGIC: The competitor (unweighted Tallying) predicts p(A) as a function of the raw tally margin d = (#A cue wins) - (#B cue wins) ONLY. My advocated theory (validity-weighted tallying) predicts p(A) as a function of the validity-weighted margin m = sum_j v_j^gamma * sign(a_j - b_j) ONLY. The design therefore decorrelates d and m: it holds d fixed while varying m, which yields two parameter-free knife predictions for the competitor and a graded dose-response for my theory. Cues: 6 experts, validities [0.99, 0.90, 0.80, 0.70, 0.60, 0.51] (maximal spread to maximize the achievable m-range; weights v_j^gamma live in [0.61, 1] over gamma in [0.05, 0.7]). DISSOCIATION 1 (parameter-free knife at d=0): Trials Z1-Z4, Z1', Z4', ZC all have exactly tied tallies (3 wins vs 3, or 2 vs 2 with ties). The competitor must predict p(A) = 0.50 EXACTLY on all seven, for every (beta, epsilon) -- a tied softmax is uniform and the lapse injects uniform. My theory predicts a graded ladder in m: at gamma=0.4, m = +0.42 (Z1), +0.33 (Z2), +0.24 (Z3), +0.12 (Z4), giving p(A) = sigmoid(2*beta*m) strictly increasing (e.g., beta=0.25: 0.553, 0.541, 0.530, 0.516; at gamma=0.7, beta=0.55: 0.680, 0.645, 0.605, 0.555). Z1' and Z4' mirror the ladder endpoints (m = -0.42, -0.12) testing sign symmetry, and ZC is a near-zero-m control (A wins cues 1 and 6, B wins cues 2 and 5; v1+v6 = v2+v5 = 1.50, so m ~ -0.01 for all gamma) where BOTH theories predict ~0.50 -- this rules out a generic 'follow the highest-validity cue' strategy (which would pick A on ZC) and generic tied-trial side bias, isolating pure validity weighting. Any systematic deviation from 0.50 on Z1/Z1' falsifies the competitor outright with no free parameters; any nonzero slope of p(A) against m across Z4->Z1 falsifies it as a dose-response. DISSOCIATION 2 (parameter-free within-d flatness): Trials P1, P3, P4 all have d = +1 (3 cue wins vs 2, one tie) and trials N1-N4 all have d = -1. The competitor must predict the IDENTICAL p(A) on P1/P3/P4 (and on N1-N4) for every parameter setting -- only the count matters. My theory predicts a strong within-d ladder: at gamma=0.4, m = 1.19 (P1: A wins the three best experts), 0.70 (P3), 0.49 (P4: A wins the three WORST experts, B wins the two best) -> p(A) = 0.644, 0.587, 0.561 at beta=0.25, spreading to 0.81 vs 0.55 at gamma=0.7, beta=0.55. A 15-25 point spread where the competitor demands exact equality is the sharpest quantitative signature of validity weighting. Note P4 is doubly diagnostic: A wins the majority of cues but only the low-validity ones, so the two theories still agree on the choice while disagreeing sharply on confidence -- pure quantitative dissociation. DISSOCIATION 3 (cross-family m-matching): Z1 (d=0, m~0.42-0.69) vs P4 (d=+1, m~0.16-0.49) nearly match m while mismatching d; the competitor predicts a large gap (sigmoid(2*beta) vs 0.50), my theory predicts a small or even reversed gap -- an honest adversarial test of my own m-only claim. ANCHORS: G1/G2 (d = +/-3, all four best experts vs one worst) let both theories agree at high confidence and pin down beta and epsilon; notably, at my claimed regime beta~0.25, G1 predicts only ~0.81-0.89, while the competitor (beta up to 20) can go to ~1.0, so even anchor confidence separates the families quantitatively. ADVERSARIAL HONESTY: if subjects sit at exactly 0.50 across the whole d=0 family and show zero within-d m-slope, my theory's central claim (gamma > 0) is falsified and the competitor wins; the design is a clean gamma-estimation experiment because the competitor is exactly the gamma -> 0 nest of my family. 16 unique pairs x K=6 = 96 trials; sides balanced (8 A-tilted, 7 B-tilted, 1 neutral control), no all-tie trials, every trial requires comparing ratings across experts, and the descending-validity display is irrelevant to both theories (neither uses display order).

metric.metric_source:
def metric(data: pd.DataFrame) -> float:
    """Tally-following rate on decisive trials.

    For every trial, compute the raw (unweighted) tally margin
    d = (# cues where A wins) - (# cues where B wins).
    On trials with d != 0, check whether the subject's choice agrees
    with the option favored by the raw cue count (A if d > 0, B if
    d < 0). The metric is the fraction of such agreement over all
    decisive trials (d = 0 trials are excluded because the tallying
    heuristic itself is indifferent there).
    """
    df = data.reset_index(drop=True)
    n = len(df)
    if n == 0:
        return 0.5

    a_lists = df['option_a_ratings'].tolist()
    b_lists = df['option_b_ratings'].tolist()
    resp = df['response'].to_numpy(dtype=float)

    d = np.empty(n, dtype=float)
    for i in range(n):
        a = np.asarray(a_lists[i], dtype=float)
        b = np.asarray(b_lists[i], dtype=float)
        d[i] = float(np.sum(a > b) - np.sum(b > a))

    decisive = d != 0.0
    if not np.any(decisive):
        return 0.5

    dd = d[decisive]
    rr = resp[decisive]
    # Option favored by the raw tally: A (response 0) if d > 0,
    # otherwise B (response 1).
    agree = np.where(dd > 0.0, rr == 0.0, rr == 1.0)
    return float(np.mean(agree))
metric.rationale:
CORE IDEA. The competitor (unweighted Tallying) has beta in [0.1, 20]; for the overwhelming majority of that range, softmax over the tallies is essentially deterministic, so its choice on any d != 0 trial follows the raw cue count with probability (1 - epsilon) + epsilon/2, i.e. ~0.87 on average over epsilon in [0, 0.5] (and > 0.75 even at epsilon = 0.5). My advocated theory is explicitly in the UNSATURATED regime (beta <= 0.55), and its validity weights compress the effective evidence far below the raw count margin: on the d = +1 trials the weighted margin m ranges from ~1.2 (A wins the three best experts) down to ~0.0 (A wins the three WORST experts, trials T10/T14), so p(follow the tally) is only sigmoid(2*beta*m) ~ 0.5-0.75, and even the d = 3 anchors only reach ~0.96 at the extreme corner. Averaged over the advocated parameter box, the predicted tally-following rate is ~0.63-0.66, versus ~0.86-0.88 for the competitor. So this single choice rate separates the two simulated theories by ~0.22 in mean.

WHY THE VARIANCE IS TIGHT ENOUGH AT N=25. The statistic is a simple binomial proportion over 54 decisive trials per subject (96 trials minus the 42 tied-tally trials). Per-subject SD is ~0.06 (binomial) plus ~0.07-0.08 of genuine parameter heterogeneity, giving between-subject variances of roughly 0.010 (self) and 0.008 (competitor). The standardized gap at N = 25 is t ~ 8 (p ~ 1e-9), far beyond the alpha = 0.01 threshold, leaving a large safety margin even if the simulator samples parameters differently than I assume (e.g., log-uniform beta for the competitor still yields t > 3; a fixed competitor draw of beta = 0.5, epsilon = 0 still yields t > 5).

WHY IT IS NOT TRIVIAL AND IS THEORY-RELEVANT. The metric directly engages the theories' central dispute about how evidence is scaled. Under the competitor, one cue win is one unit of evidence, so a 3-vs-2 count is a decisive, near-deterministic signal. Under validity weighting, winning three low-validity cues while losing the two best ones yields a weighted margin near zero (trials T10/T12/T14), so those choices are near coin flips - exactly the validity-weighting signature. The metric also operationalizes my theory's stated claim that humans sit in the graded, unsaturated softmax regime rather than the deterministic-tally corner: if humans were deterministic tallyers, this metric would approach ~0.9; the graded-evidence account predicts ~0.65. Note the tied trials (d = 0) are excluded because both theories are indifferent there, which removes the competitor's coin-flip noise and makes the per-subject estimate maximally stable. The metric is a plain choice rate, so it is identical whether computed on one subject's 96 trials or the pooled data (no grouping of unhashable list cells is needed), satisfying both evaluation levels.

proposer_theory.description: Validity-Weighted Tallying (graded-evidence regime): people integrate evidence from ALL binary expert ratings, casting each feature a sign vote (+1 win / -1 loss / 0 tie) weighted by w_j = validity_j^gamma, summing into a zero-sum evidence score, with choice a softmax (inverse temperature beta) over the two scores plus an independent uniform lapse (epsilon). The theoretical claim added this round is about where humans sit in this family: in the UNSATURATED softmax regime. Because the evidence scores are integer-scale sign tallies, beta >= 3 already drives tanh(beta*m) ~ 1 for every unit margin, making the model behaviorally deterministic and pinning it to the tallying corner; the graded dose-response in tally margin that both experiments demand (Exp 1 metric at 44% of the deterministic-tally value; Exp 2's small positive b_d) lives at beta ~ 0.2-0.3, where p(A) is approximately linear in the tally margin. Gamma stays in a mild, provably sub-lexicographic band so that no subject leaps into the TTB regime.

def predict(parameters, state, history):
    # Validity-Weighted Tallying.
    # Stimulus: array of shape (2, n_features); row 0 = option A,
    # row 1 = option B; entries are binary expert ratings.
    # Each feature j casts a vote sign(a_j - b_j) for A's score and
    # the opposite for B's score; votes are weighted by w_j =
    # validity_j ** gamma. gamma = 0 -> unweighted Tallying;
    # gamma -> large -> lexicographic TTB (top cue dominates).
    stim = np.asarray(state, dtype=float)
    if stim.ndim != 2 or stim.shape[0] != 2:
        raise ValueError(
            f"Expects a (2, n_features) stimulus; got shape {stim.shape}."
        )

    n_features = stim.shape[1]
    val = np.asarray(parameters["validities"], dtype=float)
    if val.shape[0] != n_features:
        raise ValueError(
            f"validities length {val.shape[0]} != n_features {n_features}."
        )

    gamma = float(parameters["gamma"])
    beta = float(parameters["beta"])
    epsilon = float(parameters["epsilon"])

    a, b = stim[0], stim[1]

    # Feature-wise votes: +1 where A wins the feature, -1 where B
    # wins, 0 on ties (a tied cue is uninformative for the pair).
    votes = np.sign(a - b)

    # Validity-based weights. Since validities are in [0.5, 1.0],
    # gamma = 0 gives all-ones weights (pure Tallying); increasing
    # gamma increasingly privileges high-validity cues, with the
    # top cue dominating as gamma grows (TTB limit).
    w = np.power(val, gamma)

    # Weighted evidence scores. B's score is the mirror of A's
    # because every vote is zero-sum across the two options.
    s_a = float(np.dot(w, votes))
    scores = np.array([s_a, -s_a])

    # Numerically stable softmax over the two weighted scores.
    # When all cues tie (s_a == 0) the softmax is exactly uniform,
    # which is the correct behavior for an undiscriminating tally.
    z = beta * (scores - scores.max())
    e = np.exp(z)
    p_core = e / e.sum()

    # Independent lapse: with probability epsilon output a uniform
    # pick over the two options.
    n_opts = p_core.shape[0]
    return (1.0 - epsilon) * p_core + epsilon * (np.ones(n_opts) / n_opts)
proposer_theory.rationale: This is a minimal-diff edit of the running-best (iter 3, ACCEPTED, loss 0.1606) candidate: the mechanism code is byte-identical (w_j = validity_j^gamma sign votes, zero-sum scores, stable softmax, uniform lapse); ONLY the parameter ranges change. Why I deviate from the critic's specific numbers (beta capped 3-5, epsilon floored 0.03-0.05, gamma in [0.2, 1.0]): with zero-sum sign-vote scores the softmax input is the integer tally margin m, so p(A) = sigmoid(2*beta*m) and, in the sub-flip gamma regime, Exp 1's metric is exactly -(1-epsilon)*(1/6)[tanh(beta) + tanh(2*beta) + tanh(3*beta)]. At beta = 3 this already equals -0.4995 -- indistinguishable from beta = 10 -- so capping beta at 3-5 and flooring epsilon at 0.03-0.05 leaves Exp 1 pinned at ~-0.45 (the iter-3 corner), moving it at most ~0.02 toward the real -0.218; the gate would reject. The lever the critic's diagnosis points at but its numbers don't reach is the UNSATURATED softmax regime: the real Exp 1 value (-0.218 = 44% of the deterministic-tally value -0.50) requires (1/6)*sum(tanh(k*beta)) ~ 0.44, i.e. beta ~ 0.24; independently, Exp 2's b_d must equal ~0.077, and b_d(beta) ~ 0.08 exactly at beta ~ 0.2 (b_d(0.1)=0.048, b_d(0.23)=0.091, b_d(0.5)=0.128 on the Exp 2 design). Both experiments' targets sit in the SAME low-beta band -- a joint consistency check that this is where the data live, and precisely the 'graded dose-response in tally margin' the arbiter prescribed this family to capture (at beta ~ 0.25, p(A) ~ 0.5 + 0.24*d, linear in margin). Hence beta: [0.03, 0.55]. Variance: the critic correctly flagged that iter 3 undershot the between-subject variances (0.0050 / 0.0008 vs real 0.0140 / 0.0031). With per-subject parameter sampling, spreading beta over [0.03, 0.55] makes subject-level Exp 1 metrics range from ~-0.03 to ~-0.36 (between-subject sd ~ 0.10, var ~ 0.010) which, added to within-subject binomial noise (~0.005), lands at ~0.013-0.015 -- matching the real 0.0140 without iter 1's blowup (0.0635, caused by gamma wandering across cue-flip thresholds). Gamma stays in a mild band [0.05, 0.7]: for validities in [0.5, 1.0], at any gamma <= 1 two opposing cues always out-weigh one top cue (2*0.5^gamma >= 1 >= v0^gamma), so no simulated subject can flip into the TTB regime that ruined iter 1; gamma instead gently compresses the weighted margins at low beta and injects the small top-cue effect (b_s > 0 in Exp 2) that trims +0.124 toward +0.077. Epsilon stays small ([0.0, 0.08], mean attenuation ~4%) so it calibrates rather than drives. Expected landing zone: Exp 1 ~ -0.21 (var ~ 0.013) and Exp 2 ~ +0.08 (var ~ 0.002) vs real (-0.218, 0.0140) / (+0.077, 0.0031) -- an order-of-magnitude improvement over the base's deltas (+0.243 / +0.047), with every deviation the critic listed (Exp 1 overshoot, both variance undershoots) moved in the correcting direction.

experiment.rationale: ADVOCATED THEORY: unweighted Tallying (choice depends ONLY on the raw tally margin d = #A-cue-wins - #B-cue-wins, with unbounded beta up to 20). COMPETITOR: validity-weighted tallying whose own theoretical claim pins it to a bounded box: gamma in [0.05, 0.7], beta in [0.03, 0.55], epsilon in [0, 0.08] ('unsaturated regime'). The design exploits two structural facts about that box. FACT 1 (HARD CEILINGS): the competitor's maximum achievable confidence on a trial is (1-eps)*sigmoid(2*beta*m) with m = sum_j v_j^gamma*sign(a_j-b_j). Because beta <= 0.55 and any single cue's weight is <= 1, on ANY trial where exactly one more cue favors A than B and only one cue discriminates (S1, S2), m <= 0.9995, so the competitor's absolute ceiling is p(A) = 0.750 -- no parameter setting in its box can exceed it. On minimal-m d=+2 (A wins only the two lowest-validity cues, L2) the ceiling is 0.894, and on minimal-m d=+3 (L3) it is 0.961. Tallying, with beta up to 20, can predict ~0.99 on all of these. So if subjects choose the count-winner on >80% of S1/S2 trials or >92% of L2 trials, the competitor is falsified outright with zero free parameters -- the exact mirror-image knife of Experiment [2], but aimed at the bounded regime rather than at gamma. FACT 2 (MINIMAL-m LADDER): on the ladder S2 -> L2 -> L3 every A-win is on a low-validity cue, so the competitor's evidence per tally step is only ~0.62-0.97 of a raw count unit; its steepest possible psychometric slope in d is 2*0.55*0.97 ~ 1.07 logits per step, whereas Tallying's is 2*beta, unbounded. A subject psychometric function in d that is steeper than ~1.07 logits/unit (e.g., 0.75 at d=1 rising to ~0.99 at d=3) exceeds the competitor's box. DISSOCIATION FAMILY d=+/-1 (S1, S2, S3, S4 and mirrors): all four A-tilted trials have d = +1, so Tallying makes the PARAMETER-FREE prediction p(S1)=p(S2)=p(S3)=p(S4) exactly, for every (beta, epsilon). The competitor predicts a large within-d spread because m differs sharply across compositions: at gamma=0.7, beta=0.55 its predictions are S1=0.749, S2=0.665, S4=0.816, and -- the sharpest cell -- S3=0.389, i.e., BELOW 0.50. S3 is the sign-flip trial: A wins the four weakest experts (v=0.54,0.53,0.52,0.51) while B wins the three super-experts (v=0.99,0.98,0.97); the raw count favors A (4 vs 3) but the validity-weighted margin at high gamma is m = -0.41, so the competitor predicts a B preference while Tallying predicts the same strong A preference as on S1. Subject behavior on S3 is a direct gamma-map: p(A) near p(S1) kills the competitor twice (ceiling violation + zero validity weighting); p(A) < 0.50 falsifies Tallying on a choice (not just confidence) measure. The validity vector [0.99, 0.98, 0.97, 0.55, 0.54, 0.53, 0.52, 0.51] is engineered for this: the top-two/top-three weights (0.993+0.986+0.979 = 2.958 at gamma=0.7) exceed any three or four low-cue weights (e.g., 2.548 for the four lowest), which is what makes the sign flip achievable at all with binary cues. HONEST ADVERSARIAL KNIVES AGAINST MY OWN THEORY: (i) T0 (d=0: A wins the three super-experts, B wins the three worst): Tallying MUST predict exactly 0.50 (tied softmax is uniform and the lapse injects uniform), while the competitor predicts p(A) up to 0.76 -- any systematic A-bias on T0 falsifies Tallying with no parameters; (ii) the within-d=1 spread S3<S2<S1<S4 and the L2-vs-M2 comparison (both d=+2; Tallying demands exact equality, competitor predicts L2 < M2 by up to ~10 points since M2's wins are on the two super-experts, m ~ 2.0 vs 1.26-1.93) are the competitor's best cells, included deliberately; (iii) displaying the three ~99% experts first maximizes validity salience, favoring the competitor's processing assumptions. ANCHORS: G+/G- (d = +/-6) are near-agreement trials (both theories ~1) that pin lapse rates; even here the competitor's epsilon <= 0.08 forces p in [0.958, 0.998] on G+, so an anchor error rate above ~5% strains it while Tallying's epsilon up to 0.5 absorbs any sloppiness. PREDICTED PATTERN IF MY THEORY IS RIGHT: flat near-ceiling performance across the entire d=1 family (all four compositions equal, ~0.95+), steep sigmoid in d reaching ~0.99 by d=3, exactly 0.50 on T0, L2 = M2. PREDICTED PATTERN IF THE COMPETITOR IS RIGHT: graded 0.65-0.75 on d=1 with a 15-40 point within-d spread, S3 at or below 0.50, shallow d-slope, A-bias on T0. The two patterns are disjoint almost everywhere: 16 unique pairs x K=6 = 96 trials; sides balanced (8 count-favors-A, 7 count-favors-B, 1 tied); no all-tie trials; every trial requires scanning all 8 experts to locate discriminators.

def metric(data: pd.DataFrame) -> float:
    """Hard-ceiling test on the |d|=1 family (FACT 1 of the design).

    Metric = proportion of choices that agree with the UNWEIGHTED tally
    count-winner, restricted to trials whose raw tally margin is exactly
    +/-1 (the 8 trial types t1-t8; 48 of the 96 trials per subject).

    Tallying (any beta >= 1, any epsilon) predicts ~1 - epsilon/2 here,
    i.e. >= ~0.85 for any moderate lapse. The validity-weighted
    competitor is structurally capped: its choice probability on a |d|=1
    trial is (1-eps)*sigmoid(2*beta*m) with m = sum_j v_j^gamma*sign diff;
    the mean of |m| over the 8 |d|=1 trial types is <= 1 for every
    gamma in [0.05, 0.7] (equality only at gamma=0), and beta <= 0.55,
    so by concavity of tanh its mean agreement on this family is
    <= 0.5 + tanh(0.55)/2 = 0.750 over its ENTIRE parameter box.
    """
    def _mat(col):
        vals = []
        for v in col:
            if isinstance(v, np.ndarray):
                vals.append(v)
            else:
                vals.append(list(v))
        return np.asarray(vals, dtype=float)

    A = _mat(data["option_a_ratings"])
    B = _mat(data["option_b_ratings"])
    resp = np.asarray(data["response"], dtype=float)

    if A.ndim != 2 or A.shape[0] == 0 or A.shape != B.shape:
        return 0.5

    # Raw (unweighted) tally margin per trial.
    d = (A > B).sum(axis=1) - (B > A).sum(axis=1)

    # The |d| = 1 family: 8 unique pairs x 6 reps = 48 trials/subject.
    mask = np.abs(d) == 1
    if mask.sum() < 10:
        # Defensive fallback: use all non-tied trials.
        mask = d != 0
    if mask.sum() == 0:
        return 0.5

    dm = d[mask]
    rm = resp[mask]
    # Count-winner is A when d>0 (response 0), B when d<0 (response 1).
    consistent = np.where(dm > 0, rm == 0, rm == 1)
    return float(np.mean(consistent))
metric.rationale: This metric implements the HARD-CEILING knife (FACT 1) of the design on the trial family where the two theories are maximally separated in a parameter-robust way. On every trial with raw tally margin |d|=1 (trial types t1-t8: single top-cue discriminator, single low-cue discriminator, 4-low-vs-3-top sign-flip pair, 2-top-vs-1-low pair, and their mirrors; 48 of 96 trials per subject), the competitor's predicted agreement with the count-winner is (1-eps)*sigmoid(2*beta*m) with m = sum_j v_j^gamma * sign(a_j - b_j). Because gamma <= 0.7, beta <= 0.55, epsilon <= 0.08, and the mean of |m| across the 8 trial types is at most 1 (it equals 1 only in the gamma->0 limit and shrinks as gamma grows, since the low-validity discriminators lose weight), concavity of tanh bounds the competitor's expected value on this metric by 0.5 + tanh(0.55)/2 = 0.750 over its ENTIRE box — and at its self-described operating point (beta ~ 0.25-0.3, mild gamma) it sits near 0.55-0.62. Tallying, in contrast, predicts (1-eps)*sigmoid(2*beta) + eps/2 on every one of these trials: for any beta >= 1 (most of its [0.1, 20] range) this is >= 0.88*(1-eps) + eps/2, i.e. roughly 0.85-0.95 for moderate lapses. So the theories make almost disjoint predictions on this scalar, and the gap (~0.3 in typical parameterizations, >= 0.12 even in the competitor's most favorable corner gamma->0, beta=0.55) is large relative to per-subject noise: each subject contributes 48 Bernoulli trials, so the per-subject standard deviation is only ~0.05 (tallying-like data) to ~0.10 (competitor-like data), giving Welch t on the order of 10-20 at N=25. The metric is well-defined both on the pooled data and on each single subject's slice (every subject sees all 8 |d|=1 trial types 6 times), so the between-subject variance is a proper binomial-style variance rather than n/a. It is not trivially fixed under my own theory (its value depends on beta and epsilon, and would drop toward 0.5 if subjects did not tally), and on human data it directly adjudicates the theories' conflicting predictions: near-ceiling count-winner adherence on minimal-margin trials falsifies the bounded unsaturated-regime claim, while values pinned below 0.75 falsify high-beta tallying.

proposer_theory.description: People compare two options by counting, across all features, how often one option has a higher value than the other. The option that wins on more features is chosen. Tallying discards cardinal magnitudes — only the sign of each feature-wise comparison matters — so the heuristic is robust to monotone rescaling of individual features and cannot be swayed by a single large feature difference in the way Equal-Weight can. Ties on an individual feature contribute nothing to either count: that cue is simply treated as uninformative for the pair. No feature is privileged, in contrast to Take The Best; every cue contributes equally to the tally. When the two counts are equal the heuristic has no basis for preference and the learner must guess. Response noise enters through a softmax over the two tallies with inverse temperature beta (interpolating between fully deterministic choice at large beta and uniform guessing at beta = 0), plus an independent lapse that with probability epsilon replaces the softmax output with a uniform pick over the two options.

def predict(parameters, stimulus, history):
    # Paper-faithful Tallying heuristic (Dawes 1979; Gigerenzer &
    # Goldstein 1999). Stimulus is the pair of option feature vectors
    # for the current trial: array-like of shape (2, n_features),
    # with row 0 = option A, row 1 = option B. History is ignored.
    stim = np.asarray(stimulus, dtype=float)
    if stim.ndim != 2 or stim.shape[0] != 2:
        raise ValueError(
            f"Tallying expects a (2, n_features) stimulus; got shape {stim.shape}."
        )

    a, b = stim[0], stim[1]
    # Count strict feature-wise wins; ties contribute to neither option.
    a_wins = float(np.sum(a > b))
    b_wins = float(np.sum(b > a))
    scores = np.array([a_wins, b_wins])

    beta = float(parameters["beta"])
    epsilon = float(parameters["epsilon"])

    # Softmax with max-subtraction for numerical stability. When
    # a_wins == b_wins the softmax is exactly uniform regardless of
    # beta, which is the correct behavior for an undiscriminating
    # tally.
    z = beta * (scores - scores.max())
    e = np.exp(z)
    p_core = e / e.sum()

    n_opts = p_core.shape[0]
    return (1.0 - epsilon) * p_core + epsilon * (np.ones(n_opts) / n_opts)

next_theory.description: Flattened-Diagnosticity Evidence Integration (the extreme-compression corner of the Bayesian cue-counting family): people integrate ALL binary expert ratings into one evidence score, where each discriminating cue casts a sign vote weighted by w_j = max(log(v_j/(1-v_j)) - tau, 0)^delta — chance cues (v=0.5) are annihilated exactly, but among genuinely diagnostic cues the subjective weight is a HEAVILY flattened (delta ~ 0.15) version of the normative log-odds, and choice is a low-gain softmax (2*beta ~ 0.6) plus a small uniform lapse. The new theoretical claim is that the compression exponent delta is itself the structural margin-compression device: shrinking delta equalizes weights, which GROWS count-dominated conflict margins (where cues split across options) while SHRINKING alignment-dominated cumulative margins (where several strong cues pile onto one side). This differential action — not any global gain knob, and not trial-level normalization — is what lets a single small beta simultaneously produce moderate TTB-leaning conflict-trial behavior (Exp 1), a slightly positive tally-vs-top-cue regression slope (Exp 2), graded ~0.62 tally-following (Exp 3), and near-chance |d|=1 agreement driven by the cancellation between super-expert matches and super-expert reversals (Exp 4).

def predict(parameters, state, history):
    # Diagnosticity-Weighted Evidence Integration (Bayesian cue-counting).
    # Stimulus: array of shape (2, n_features); row 0 = option A,
    # row 1 = option B; entries are binary expert ratings (0/1).
    # Each feature j casts a sign vote sign(a_j - b_j); the vote is
    # weighted by the cue's log-likelihood-ratio diagnosticity
    # llr_j = log(v_j / (1 - v_j)), rectified by an attention floor
    # tau and compressed by an exponent delta:
    #   w_j = (max(llr_j - tau, 0))^delta
    # A v = 0.5 expert has llr = 0 -> exactly zero evidence.
    stim = np.asarray(state, dtype=float)
    if stim.ndim != 2 or stim.shape[0] != 2:
        raise ValueError(
            f"Expects a (2, n_features) stimulus; got shape {stim.shape}."
        )

    n_features = stim.shape[1]
    val = np.asarray(parameters["validities"], dtype=float)
    if val.shape[0] != n_features:
        raise ValueError(
            f"validities length {val.shape[0]} != n_features {n_features}."
        )

    delta = float(parameters["delta"])
    tau = float(parameters["tau"])
    beta = float(parameters["beta"])
    epsilon = float(parameters["epsilon"])

    a, b = stim[0], stim[1]

    # Feature-wise votes: +1 where A wins the feature, -1 where B
    # wins, 0 on ties (a tied cue is uninformative for the pair).
    votes = np.sign(a - b)

    # Normative diagnosticity: log-likelihood-ratio of each expert.
    # Clip away from v = 1.0 to keep the log finite; v = 0.5 maps to 0.
    v = np.clip(val, 0.5, 1.0 - 1e-9)
    llr = np.log(v / (1.0 - v))

    # Limited-attention floor: diagnosticity below tau is discarded;
    # the remainder is compressed by the exponent delta. delta = 1 is
    # the purely normative Bayesian weight; delta < 1 flattens the
    # diagnosticity gradient toward tallying over informative cues
    # (while v = 0.5 cues stay annihilated at any delta, since
    # llr(0.5) = 0 <= tau); delta > 1 sharpens it toward
    # lexicographic/TTB-like use of the best experts.
    w = np.power(np.maximum(llr - tau, 0.0), delta)

    # Weighted evidence score. B's score is the mirror of A's because
    # every vote is zero-sum across the two options.
    s_a = float(np.dot(w, votes))
    scores = np.array([s_a, -s_a])

    # Numerically stable low-temperature softmax. When all attended
    # cues tie (s_a == 0) the softmax is exactly uniform, which is the
    # correct behavior for undiscriminating evidence.
    z = beta * (scores - scores.max())
    e = np.exp(z)
    p_core = e / e.sum()

    # Independent lapse: with probability epsilon output a uniform
    # pick over the two options.
    n_opts = p_core.shape[0]
    return (1.0 - epsilon) * p_core + epsilon * (np.ones(n_opts) / n_opts)
next_theory.rationale: MINIMAL-DIFF EDIT: the code is the accepted iter-2 base VERBATIM; the only change is the parameter box (delta, tau, beta, epsilon). I accept the critic's iter-3 DIAGNOSIS in full (Exps 3/4 are saturated by large cumulative margins; Exps 1/2 need more effective gain; no global beta/epsilon can serve both) but I reject its prescribed FIX (kappa normalization) on quantitative grounds, and I reject the delta floor of ~0.35 as well. (1) WHY KAPPA HAS THE WRONG SIGN. Normalization divides the margin by (sum of discriminating weights)^kappa. Exp 1's conflict trials have 3-4 discriminators splitting across options (net weighted margin ~0.6-0.9, total weight ~3.6-4.2), so kappa=1 compresses their effective signal to ~0.17-0.25 — exactly the trials that need MORE gain. Exp 4's single-super-expert |d|=1 types have one discriminator, so m_norm = w0/w0^kappa = w0^(1-kappa), i.e. exactly 1 at kappa=1 — unsaturable only at beta ~ 0.1, which collapses Exp 1 to ~-0.01. Kappa compresses the trials that need gain and spares the trials that need compression: the opposite of the required differential action. (2) THE CORRECT IN-FAMILY STRUCTURAL KNOB IS DELTA ITSELF. Shrinking delta from 0.5 to 0.15 equalizes weights: count-dominated conflict margins GROW (Exp 1 type-1: -0.62 -> -0.91, because the tally side's cue count reasserts itself) while alignment-dominated cumulative margins SHRINK (Exp 4's super-expert sum W = w0+w1+w2: 4.8 -> 3.4). The ratio W/conflict drops from ~5 to ~2.6, so ONE small gain (2*beta ~ 0.6) puts Exp 1 conflicts at tanh ~ 0.27-0.49, Exp 4 matches at sigma ~ 0.65-0.82, and — critically — Exp 4's reversed types (three super-experts opposing the raw tally) at 1-sigma(2*beta*W) ~ 0.10-0.16, whose cancellation against the matches is what holds the |d|=1 metric near 0.51 instead of the saturated 0.58-0.60 of iter 2. (3) VALIDATION OF THE ALGEBRA. Applying the same margin-level computation at the ACCEPTED iter-2 box center (delta 0.4, beta 0.65) reproduces that candidate's actual outputs almost exactly: predicted Exp 1 = -0.288 vs actual -0.2795; predicted Exp 4 = 0.583 vs actual 0.5796. The algebra is therefore trustworthy, and it identifies (delta ~ 0.15, beta ~ 0.3) as the simultaneous optimum: Exp 1 ~ -0.21 to -0.22 (target -0.218), Exp 2 ~ +0.06 (target +0.077; near-equal weights keep b_d positive while the small cue-0 tilt keeps b_s small), Exp 3 ~ 0.61-0.63 (target 0.617), Exp 4 ~ 0.52 (target 0.513). (4) WHY THIS IS NOT OSCILLATION. The delta box [0.10, 0.20] extends the ACCEPTED base's [0.20, 0.6] downward — it is not a return to the critic's rejected delta~1 regime — and the annihilation property (llr(0.5)=0 <= tau for every tau in the box) is preserved everywhere, so the validated Exp 4 mechanism survives intact. The beta box [0.27, 0.37] is the critic's requested restoration of gain, rescaled to the ~2.5x smaller margins that delta-compression produces (equivalent effective gain to the critic's [0.35, 1.0] at delta 0.5). Expected residuals: |Exp1| ~ 0.01, |Exp2| ~ 0.02, |Exp3| ~ 0.01-0.03, |Exp4| ~ 0.01 — every one at or below the accepted base's residuals (0.062, 0.026, 0.050, 0.066), with the two dominant errors (Exp 1 and Exp 4) essentially eliminated.

experiment.rationale: CORE LOGIC. The two theories share the same architecture (sign votes x weights x softmax) and differ ONLY in the weight function. The one validity where they are structurally disjoint is v = 0.5: the competitor's weight is max(llr - tau, 0)^delta with llr(0.5) = 0, so a 50%-accurate expert is annihilated EXACTLY (weight 0) for every (delta, tau, beta, epsilon) in its box. My advocated theory gives it weight 0.5^gamma in [0.62, 0.97] -- i.e., 62-97% of a super-expert's weight. The design therefore builds everything around three chance experts (v = 0.5) set against one near-chance diagnostic expert (v = 0.55) and one super-expert (v = 0.95), using 8 features: [0.95, 0.85, 0.75, 0.65, 0.55, 0.50, 0.50, 0.50]. DISSOCIATION 1 (parameter-free knife: chance-only trials). Trials Z1-Z3 and mirror Z1m have ONLY v=0.5 cues discriminating. The competitor must predict p(A) = 0.50 EXACTLY on all four (all weights zero -> uniform softmax, and the lapse also injects uniform) for every parameter setting. My theory predicts a strictly graded ladder in the net chance-cue count k: p(A) = sigmoid(2*beta*0.5^gamma*k); at representative (beta=0.25, gamma=0.4): Z3 = 0.59, Z2 = 0.68, Z1 = 0.76 (range across my box: 0.51-0.96, always > 0.5 for k > 0). Any systematic deviation from 0.50 on Z trials, or any nonzero slope of p(A) against k, falsifies the competitor outright with no free parameters. DISSOCIATION 2 (parameter-free flatness + robust sign flip: super-expert vs chance-cue dose). Trials X0-X3 hold the diagnostic structure fixed (B wins the v=0.95 expert; for the competitor the chance cues contribute exactly nothing) while the net chance-cue count for A varies 0, 1, 2, 3. The competitor must predict the IDENTICAL p(A) on X0, X3, X2, X1 for all parameters -- its entire box spans only p(A) in [0.29, 0.36]. My theory predicts a strictly monotone ladder crossing 0.5: at (beta=0.25, gamma=0.4): X0 = 0.38, X3 = 0.47, X2 = 0.57, X1 = 0.66. Critically, on X1 and X2 the SIGN of preference disagrees robustly across BOTH entire parameter boxes: my theory predicts p(A) > 0.5 for every admissible (gamma, beta) (minimum 0.52), the competitor predicts p(A) < 0.5 for every admissible (delta, tau, beta, epsilon) (maximum 0.36). Mirrors Xm1, Xm2 flip sides and control for side bias. DISSOCIATION 3 (threshold structure of the 0.55 expert -- includes an honest knife against my own theory). The competitor treats v=0.55 as a genuinely diagnostic cue with weight 0.72-0.85 (about 60-75% of the super-expert's weight), while my theory treats 0.55 and 0.5 as nearly identical (weight ratio (0.5/0.55)^gamma in [0.94, 1.0]). W1 (A wins the 0.55 cue, B wins one 0.5 cue): my theory predicts p(A) <= 0.52 across its ENTIRE box (the validity difference is at most 0.042 in weighted units, so even beta = 0.55 yields only 0.523); the competitor predicts 0.59-0.65. This cell alone can falsify MY theory -- included deliberately. W2/W3 (A wins 2 or 3 chance cues, B wins the 0.55 cue): my theory predicts an increasing A-ladder (0.59 -> 0.68 at representative params; >= 0.52 across the box); the competitor predicts p(A) = 0.36-0.41, and moreover demands W2 = W3 EXACTLY (both equal -w(0.55) in evidence) -- a second parameter-free flatness knife. Wm2 mirrors W2. So the W family pits the competitor's sharp 0.5/0.55 threshold against my theory's near-equal weighting: the competitor demands W1 = 1 - W2 = 1 - W3 with W2 = W3; my theory demands W1 ~ 0.50 with W2 < W3 strictly. ANCHORS. G1/G1m (four best experts vs the 0.55 expert) are agreement trials pinning beta and epsilon (my theory ~0.81/~0.19; competitor ~0.90/~0.10 at representative params -- even anchor confidence mildly separates them). KEY QUANTITATIVE METRICS: (i) slope of p(A) on net chance-cue wins k at fixed diagnostic opposition (Z family and X family): exactly 0 for the competitor, ~0.08-0.10 per cue for my theory at the claimed unsaturated regime (beta ~ 0.25); (ii) the sign of p(A)-0.5 on X1/X2/W2: positive for all my parameters, negative for all competitor parameters; (iii) p(W1): mine <= 0.52, competitor >= 0.59 -- disjoint intervals, a two-sided knife. PREDICTED PATTERN IF MY THEORY IS RIGHT: graded chance-cue dose-response everywhere (Z ladder 0.59/0.68/0.76; X ladder 0.38/0.47/0.57/0.66; W ladder 0.50/0.59/0.68 at representative params), i.e., subjects treat 50%-accurate experts as carrying most of a super-expert's weight. IF THE COMPETITOR IS RIGHT: exact 0.50 on all Z trials, flat 0.32 across the X family, W1 = 0.62 with W2 = W3 = 0.38, i.e., subjects exactly annihilate chance experts and sharply distinguish 0.55 from 0.50. The patterns are disjoint almost everywhere. 16 unique pairs x K = 6 = 96 trials; sides balanced (8 A-tilted, 7 B-tilted, 1 near-neutral); no all-tie trials; every trial requires scanning all 8 experts to locate discriminators; the three 50% experts are announced up front, so the design is a fair test of whether explicitly chance information is integrated or annihilated.
